title: 2 Kings
subtitle: Two kingdoms fall
lead: 2 Kings picks up where 1 Kings stops, with no break in the story. King Ahaziah of Israel falls through a window and sends to ask a foreign god if he will live. Elijah answers for the LORD, and soon a whirlwind carries Elijah into the sky. His follower Elisha takes up his cloak, and for eight chapters one miracle follows another: oil that keeps pouring, a dead boy raised, a foreign general healed of skin disease, an iron ax head that floats.

Then the long fall begins. Jehu wipes out Ahab's family, Assyria rises, and in 722 BC Samaria falls and the northern kingdom of Israel is carried away. Judah lasts more than a century longer, through the good kings Hezekiah and Josiah and the bad king Manasseh. In 586 BC Babylon burns Jerusalem and its temple. The book closes in exile, with one small sign of hope: Judah's captive king is let out of prison and given a seat at the Babylonian king's table.
facts: Not named. Jewish tradition (Bavli Bava Batra 15a): the prophet Jeremiah wrote Kings. Most critical scholars: the last part of the Deuteronomistic History, first written or edited under Josiah (late 7th century BC) and completed in the exile, from sources it names, such as the records of the kings of Israel and of Judah (1:18; 8:23).
Set about 853–561 BC, from Ahaziah of Israel to the release of Jehoiachin in Babylon (25:27). The book reached its final form after 561 BC, in the exile.
Samaria and Jerusalem; Elisha's places (Jericho, Bethel, Gilgal, Shunem, Mount Carmel, Dothan); Moab, Edom, Damascus, and the empires of Assyria, Egypt and Babylon.

Historical narrative on a framework of king-by-king summaries, with prophetic stories (the Elijah and Elisha cycles, Isaiah and Hezekiah), a sermon on the fall of Samaria (17:7–23) and Josiah's reform (22–23).

Hebrew. The Greek Septuagint calls it 4 Kingdoms (4 Reigns). For all of 2 Kings the main Greek manuscript, Codex Vaticanus, has a 'kaige' text revised toward the Hebrew; the Lucianic (Antiochene) Greek keeps more of the Old Greek.
25 chapters, 719 verses. 1 and 2 Kings were one book in Hebrew; the Vulgate calls this book 4 Kings.

audience.to: Judeans who had lost their land, their king and their Temple. Most scholars think the book was finished in the exile, after Jehoiachin's release in 561 BC (25:27), for exiles in Babylon and the remnant left in Judah. Many also think a first edition was written in Jerusalem under Josiah (about 620 BC), for a Judah in the middle of reform, while Assyria was falling.
audience.why: To answer the question every exile asked: how could the LORD's chosen people lose the land, the city and the house where he put his name? Kings answers that Israel and then Judah broke the covenant of Moses and would not listen to prophet after prophet, so the fall was just, and was foretold (17:7–23; 21:10–15). But the book also keeps a door open. The LORD spares Judah for David's sake (8:19), hears the prayers of humbled kings (22:19), and the last scene shows David's heir alive and honored in Babylon (25:27–30). Knowing the first readers were exiles changes how the stories read. Elisha's wonders show the LORD at work outside palaces and Temple, even among foreigners like Naaman. Hezekiah's prayer and Josiah's reform show what turning back looks like. The long list of kings is a mirror held up to a people asking whether they, too, will listen.
views: Jeremiah or a prophet of his circle

The Talmud (Bavli Bava Batra 15a) says Jeremiah wrote Kings. On this view the first readers were Jeremiah's own generation, in Judah and in exile, and the book is a prophet's explanation of the disaster he had warned about. The near copy of 24:18–25:30 in Jeremiah 52 is often cited.

Martin Noth read Deuteronomy through Kings as one work written in the exile, about 550 BC, to show the exiles that their punishment was deserved. He saw little hope in it beyond accepting God's judgment.

Frank Moore Cross and many others see a first edition under Josiah, written to back his reform and his claim to the north, with Josiah as the new David (23:25). A second, exilic edition added the end and the blame on Manasseh, for readers who had seen the reform fail.

Gerhard von Rad and others stress the release of Jehoiachin (25:27–30) and the promise to David. On this view the book was meant to keep the exiles turning back to the LORD and waiting. Jon Levenson reads the last four verses as a quiet sign that David's line has a future.

Rudolf Smend and his students see a basic exilic history (DtrH) revised by later editors, one adding prophetic material (DtrP) and one stressing the law (DtrN). Each later editor updated the work for exiles with new concerns.

lenses.name: History as told
lenses.desc: The traditional reading, Jewish and Christian: the book continues the court records of Israel and Judah from Ahaziah (about 853 BC) to the fall of Samaria (722) and of Jerusalem (586), with prophets such as Elisha and Isaiah as God's witnesses. Jewish tradition credits Jeremiah with writing Kings (Bava Batra 15a).

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read 2 Kings as the end of the Deuteronomistic History. Many see a first edition under Josiah, which made his reform the climax, and a second edition in the exile that explained the fall of Jerusalem. The Elisha stories are often read as older prophetic legends gathered into the history.

lenses.name: Ancient records
lenses.desc: Outside sources touch this book more than any other in the Hebrew Bible: the Mesha Stele (chapter 3), the Tel Dan stele and Jehu on the Black Obelisk (chapters 9–10), Assyrian annals of Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser and Sargon (15–17), Sennacherib's Prism and the Lachish reliefs (18–19), Hezekiah's Tunnel (20:20), and the Babylonian Chronicle and Jehoiachin's ration tablets (24–25). Scholars still debate how they fit together.

lenses.name: Jewish tradition
lenses.desc: The rabbis see in Elisha a double portion of Elijah's spirit, honor Hezekiah and Josiah as the great reforming kings, and mourn the Temple's fall on Tisha B'Av. The book ends with a captive king released from prison, read as a sign that David's line would endure.

lenses.name: Christian
lenses.desc: Jesus points to Elisha healing the foreigner Naaman (Luke 4:27), and many Christian readers see Elisha's miracles, such as raising a boy and feeding a hundred people, as signs that look ahead to Jesus' own. Jesus' genealogy runs through the kings of Judah and the exile (Matthew 1:6–12).

authorship: Traditional view: Jeremiah and the prophets

The Talmud says that Jeremiah wrote the book of Kings (Bavli Bava Batra 15a), and 1 and 2 Kings were one book in Hebrew. The last chapters of 2 Kings (24:18–25:30) are repeated almost word for word in Jeremiah 52, and the two books share much language. Kings points readers to the records of the kings of Israel and of Judah (1:18; 8:23) as its sources, and Chronicles names further prophetic writings, among them a vision of Isaiah for Hezekiah's reign (2 Chronicles 32:32). Traditional readers take the Elisha stories as memories handed on by the sons of the prophets, and the history as written by prophets who saw God's hand in Israel's fall.

Since Martin Noth (1943), most critical scholars read Kings as the end of a history running from Deuteronomy through 2 Kings, judging kings by Deuteronomy's demand for one place of worship. Frank Moore Cross and many others see a first edition under Josiah, which made his reform the climax (22–23), and a second edition in the exile that explained the fall of Jerusalem by Manasseh's sins (21:10–15; 23:26–27; 24:3–4). Others, following Rudolf Smend and his students, see several layers of exilic editing. The Elisha cycle (2–8; 13:14–21) and the Isaiah stories (18:13–20:19) are usually read as older prophetic material taken into the history.

Literary readers, such as Robert Cohn and Burke Long, look at how the stories are told: the threefold patterns of the Elijah and Elisha tales, the careful matching of prophecy and fulfillment, and the long arc from Elijah's ascent to Jehoiachin's release. They notice how the book sets kings beside prophets, and how its quiet ending leaves the reader in exile, waiting.

The text page beside each chapter can show several translations. Only the one you pick is loaded.

Plain English Translation

A fresh rendering made for this site from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex), at about an 8th-grade reading level. Each verse was drafted from a word-by-word gloss of the Hebrew, then checked against other English versions and redrafted wherever it followed one of them too closely. Key terms match the rest of the site and 1 Kings: YHWH is "the LORD"; YHWH tseva'ot is "the LORD of Armies" (3:14); tsara'at is "skin disease" (5:1), since it is not modern leprosy; Elijah's 'adderet is his "cloak" (2:8); and the guilds of prophets are "the sons of the prophets" (2:3). Names follow the Hebrew of each verse, so the same king may be Jehoram in one verse and Joram in the next. Where the Hebrew margin (Qere) differs from the written text (Ketiv), the notes say which is followed.

The Hebrew and the Greek 4 Kingdoms

In the Greek Septuagint this book is 4 Kingdoms. For all of 2 Kings the main Greek manuscript, Codex Vaticanus, which the standard Rahlfs edition follows, has the "kaige" text, an early Jewish revision brought close to the Hebrew. The Lucianic (Antiochene) manuscripts are the better witness to the original Old Greek, and the variants say which Greek they cite. The Greek has a few larger differences, such as a summary of Jehoram's reign after 1:18 and a different chronology for some kings, but on the whole 2 Kings has fewer major text questions than 1 Kings. Chronicles retells much of the book (2 Chronicles 21–36), Isaiah 36–39 repeats 2 Kings 18:13–20:19, and Jeremiah 52 repeats 24:18–25:30, so the parallel texts are noted where they differ. Fragments of Kings survive among the Dead Sea Scrolls, among them a papyrus from Cave 6 (6Q4) with bits of 2 Kings 5–10; they are too broken to change the text followed here.

Other translations

The Berean Standard Bible (2023), the King James Version (1611/1769), the American Standard Version (1901), Young's Literal Translation (1898) and the World English Bible can be shown for comparison.

The book continues the king-by-king framework of 1 Kings, but its weight falls in three places. Chapters 1–8 belong to the prophets: Elijah's last days and the many wonders of Elisha, set in the reigns of Ahab's sons. Chapters 9–17 run from Jehu's bloody coup to the fall of Samaria in 722 BC, ending with a sermon on why Israel fell (17:7–23). Chapters 18–25 follow Judah alone: Hezekiah's faith and Jerusalem's rescue from Sennacherib, Manasseh's evil, Josiah's reform, and the end under Babylon. Each king is again measured by whether he did what was right or evil in the LORD's eyes, northern kings by the sins of Jeroboam and southern kings by David. Prophecies are given and fulfilled throughout, and the book ends without comment, with Jehoiachin eating at the Babylonian king's table.

No book of the Hebrew Bible can be checked against so many outside sources. The Mesha Stele gives Moab's side of the revolt of chapter 3. Shalmaneser III's inscriptions name Hazael as a usurper, as 8:15 does, and his Black Obelisk shows Jehu or his envoy bowing before him. The Tel Dan stele, probably Hazael's, mentions "the house of David." Assyrian annals record tribute from Menahem, Hoshea and Hezekiah and the fall of Samaria; Sennacherib's prism and the Lachish reliefs tell of the campaign of 701 BC, and the Siloam inscription records Hezekiah's tunnel. The Babylonian Chronicle dates Jerusalem's surrender on 16 March 597 BC, and ration tablets from Babylon name Jehoiachin. Traditional scholars take this agreement as evidence that Kings used reliable court records. Critical scholars agree that the regnal framework rests on archives but read the Elisha stories as prophetic legend and note where the outside sources differ, for instance on who killed Joram and Ahaziah (9:24–27) and on the outcome of 701 BC. The chronology of the kings remains a long-standing puzzle, usually solved by co-regencies and different ways of counting.

sections.h: How Jews and Christians read 2 Kings
sections.b: In Jewish tradition 2 Kings closes the Former Prophets. Several chapters are read as haftarot: the Shunammite beside Sarah's promised son (4:1–37 with Genesis 18, Vayera), Naaman's healing beside the laws of skin disease (4:42–5:19 with Leviticus 12–13, Tazria), the four men at the gate (7:3–20 with Leviticus 14–15, Metzora), Joash's temple repairs on the Sabbath of the half-shekel (12:1–17; Sephardim 11:17–12:17), and Josiah's Passover on the second day of Passover (23:1–9, 21–25). Elijah, taken up alive, is the herald of the Messiah, and the rabbis say that Elisha did twice as many wonders as his master. Hezekiah and Josiah are honored as the great reformers, and the fall of Jerusalem is mourned on Tisha B'Av. Christians see in Elijah a pattern for John the Baptist (Luke 1:17) and in Elisha's wonders signs that point to Jesus, who cites Naaman at Nazareth (Luke 4:27). Elijah's ascension and Elisha's double share of his spirit have often been read with Jesus' ascension and the gift of the Spirit (Acts 1–2), and the line of Judah's kings runs through the exile into Jesus' genealogy (Matthew 1:7–12).

spec.title: Claude's theory: from a chariot of fire to a seat at the table
spec.body: My own reading of the whole book: 2 Kings opens with a prophet lifted out of the world in fire (2:11) and ends with a king lifted up from prison to eat at a foreign king's table (25:27–30). Between them the book tells how Israel, then Judah, lost everything that Elijah and Elisha had fought for: the land, the temple, the king's freedom. Yet both ends are acts of raising up. Several commentators have linked the two ends through the language of lifting up, since Evil-merodach "lifted the head" of Jehoiachin (25:27). I build on that: I suggest that the book's frame is deliberate: it begins with God taking his prophet up and ends with a quiet sign that God has not let David's line go down for good. On this reading the small ending answers the great beginning, and the reader in exile is meant to hope that the God who took Elijah up can raise his people again.

prompts: Elijah taken up in a storm wind (2:11–12)

On the far bank of a river, a chariot and horses made of fire sweep between two men. An old prophet in a rough hairy cloak is lifted upward in a spiral of wind; his cloak slips from his shoulders and falls. Below, a younger bald man reaches up with both arms, his mouth open in a cry, his own clothes torn. Reeds bend in the wind.

reading: Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor, II Kings (Anchor Bible, 1988)
The standard critical commentary, strongest on the Assyrian and Babylonian evidence.
T. R. Hobbs, 2 Kings (Word Biblical Commentary, 1985)
A careful commentary that takes the book's literary shape seriously and reads it as history writing.
Marvin A. Sweeney, I & II Kings (Old Testament Library, 2007)
A critical commentary attentive to the book's editions and to Jewish interpretation.
A close literary reading of how the stories are told.
A study of the Elijah and Elisha stories by type, from short legenda to longer narratives.
A short evangelical commentary that reads Kings as a carefully crafted, critical history.

A theological reading in the Christian tradition, alert to typology.
